newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-TAP must put house in order before selloff.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-TAP must put house in order before selloff.

text.p: TAP-Air Portugal, facing a selective pilots' strike from Saturday, must resolve staff problems and improve its finances and marketing in order to become a viable prospect for privatisation, analysts said.

In a bitter dispute over working hours, pilots decided on Thursday night to resume an indefinite strike. From midnight local time (2300 GMT Friday), they will refuse to operate flights not scheduled at least three days in advance.
The government has warned that the conflict with the pilots during the peak summer holiday season could lead the Portuguese state airline into bankrupcy.
"During the high season, the pilots know they have strong bargaining power," said Nigel Hawkins, transport analyst at Yamaichi International in London.
"It is in the interests of all parties to find a solution to the dispute, but it is hard to say when that will be," he added.

"Perhaps from October onwards, when the air traffic to Portugal will drop, both sides will be able to reach a long term agreement over working hours. This is a priority for the privatisation process."

The pilots say TAP employs too few of them, and that administrative staff often tell them at the last minute to change their work schedules, forcing them to fly flights after inadequate rest, jeopardising safety.

The government says it is doing all it can to satisfy the pilots' demands by pressing ahead with plans to invest 800 million escudos ($4.2 million) to upgrade its computing system used to set flights and pilots' working hours.
The standoff has destroyed morale inside the airline. Ground staff are openly critical of the pilots, accusing them of putting the jobs of the airline's 7,500 employees at risk.

Both TAP's management and the Civil Aviation Pilots' Union (SPAC), which represents all of TAP's 430 pilots, have said they are willing to continue talks to seek an end to the dispute. No further talks between the two sides were scheduled for Friday.
TAP officials said they could not forecast how many flights would be cancelled over the weekend.
Another analyst said TAP had to cut costs and debt in order to appeal to investors. The government hopes to privatise TAP, at least partially, before the end of the century.
The Portuguese state is barred by agreements with the European Union from pouring any more funds into the company.
Last April, TAP forecast that it could make a profit in 1997 for the first time in more than two decades.
But airline officials have said that the strike could affect at least 15 percent of TAP's flights and could cost the carrier at least three billion escudos in August.
Two weekends ago the pilots began their protest forcing TAP to cancel 12 flights and stranding at least 1,300 people.

The pilots then suspended the strike until 2300 GMT on Friday to continue talks with TAP's management and government officials. At a general assembly on Thursday night, they voted overwhelmingly to resume the strike after the talks failed.
TAP's pilots staged a two-day strike in April in another protest over working hours, grounding international flights and stranding 14,000 passengers.
TAP flies international routes and to the Portuguese mid-Atlantic islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Analysts were sceptical that the Portuguese government would allow its flagship carrier to go bust as TAP had good long term growth potential with demand for flights to Iberia from business people and tourists expected to rise.
Yamaichi's Hawkins said TAP had to improve its marketing in order to lure investors.
"News about strikes doesn't do TAP's image any good," he said.
($ = 188.7 Portugese Escudos)
